entries.title: Zambia after the polls: A test for democracy in Africa
entries.summary: Zambia's democratic institutions are under scrutiny, as the opposition continues to dispute the election results and courts remain closed. Weeks after the election, Zambia’s election story might be far from over.
entries.content:
Zambia

Zambia after the polls: A test for democracy

August 26, 2026

Zambia's democratic institutions are under scrutiny, as the opposition continues to dispute the election results and courts remain closed. Weeks after the election, Zambia’s election story might be far from over.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia has declared incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema winner of the August 13 presidential election.

His closest challenger, Brian Mundubile, received 38% of the vote, according to official results published last week. However, Mundubile has since announced on several occasions that he would be challenging that result, and that his National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) "shall not relent" in the face of any obstacle.

That challenge, however, comes as Zambia's courts have all remained closed since August 24 until further notice, with officials citing "security concerns."

The timing of this closure has raised questions about opposition voices having access to judicial election safeguards during this crucial stage of the post-election process, as random reports of irregularities continue to surface.

Election dispute continues to unfold

The Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) has called for the urgent restoration of access to the courts and for alternative arrangements to be enacted for urgent cases.

LAZ President Arnold Kaluba said security measures must not undermine any access to justice or judicial independence.

"Such measures must be lawful, proportionate and implemented in a manner that preserves access to justice and respects the constitutional independence and autonomy of the judiciary," he stressed.

Meanwhile, the Human Rights Commission of Zambia has also expressed concern; its chairperson, Pamela Towela Sambo, warned that disruption to judicial operations could affect fundamental rights in the country, including access to a fair trial and legal remedies.

"[If] the right to a fair trial is delayed, there is increased risk of arbitrary detentions, while access to remedies is effectively blocked," she said.

'Irregular' submission of petition documents

However, the ongoing election dispute has taken a new turn: Zambia's Chief Justice Mumba Malila, acknowledged on August 25 that he had received documents described as a presidential election petition through his private email-address.

Malila described the method of submission as "highly irregular" —despite the current circumstances allowing no access to legal procedures. He said he nevertheless referred the documents to the Constitutional Court to determine whether this qualified as a petition having been formally filed.

The distinction here is important: The receipt of such documents does not confirm that a presidential election petition has been formally lodged per se.

The latest development comes as the courts remain closed, adding to questions about how election-related cases can be filed and processed.

Government continues to cite security concerns for court closure

Meanwhile, the presidency has rejected suggestions that the court closures were intended to prevent and intervene with any challenges to the election result.

Hichilema's chief communications specialist Clayson Hamasaka said the security measures were of a "intelligence-led and preventive" nature, adding that they involved several government institutions beyond courts, and that they were intended to protect officials, institutions and members of the public.

He also maintained that people with legitimate grievances remained free to pursue remedies provided by law.

But during the election itself, there had already been suspensions of voting at some ballot boxes amid reports of violence. Questions about the independence of the media had also surface in the run-up to the vote.

Concerns about access to justice and public confidence remain strong, especially against this backdrop; the Zambia Executive Director Maurice Nyambe of Transparency International said in this context the country needs stronger institutions for resolving political disputes.

"At this stage of the electoral process, Zambia does not need fewer avenues for resolving political disputes. It needs stronger, accessible, and trusted institutions through which those disputes can be peacefully resolved."

Political commentator and human rights activist Laura Miti meanwhile questioned the lack of a fuller public explanation for the closure, writing on Facebook that "if you are going to unprecedentedly close the courts, you owe the nation an explanation beyond a blanket — there is a security threat."

A test beyond the ballot box

Zambia has long been regarded as one of Southern Africa's more stable multiparty democracies with a reputation for political stability and peaceful transfers of power.

But the current dispute comes at a time when democratic institutions across the region keep facing growing scrutiny over contested elections and political transitions. Therefore, the handling of situation will likely be observed beyond Zambia and the southern African region.

For Zambians, the issue goes beyond the contest between Hichilema and Mundubile; it is about how political disagreements can be resolved peacefully through independent, accessible and trusted institutions.

That notion is perhaps best reflected on the streets of Lusaka; a citizen of the capital simply told DW: "We are anxious and afraid because we do not know the truth about what is happening."

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: Moscow confirms visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe
entries.summary: The Russian government said that spy chief John Ratcliffe held talks with counterparts, but not President Vladimir Putin, on his Moscow trip.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

The Russian government said that spy chief John Ratcliffe held talks with counterparts, but not President Vladimir Putin, on his Moscow trip.

The Kremlin confirmed on Wednesday that US foreign intelligence chief John Ratcliffe had held a series of high-level talks the previous day in Moscow, but denied reports that he had spoken with President Vladimir Putin.

CIA Director Ratcliffe had "contacts between security services," according to Russian government spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

Peskov said that President Putin had been "informed without delay" as to the content of the talks, but had not attended the meetings.

He added that he was unsure if the discussions could move US-Russian relations out of their current "profound crisis" and would not confirm if the group had discussed the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Talks come as Iran truce stalls

Multiple US outlets reported on Ratcliffe's visit, but US President Donald Trump's administration has yet to comment on the trip. There were however photos of Ratcliffe's military plane landing in Latvia shortly before the meetings.

The last time a CIA director visited Moscow was Ratcliffe's predecessor William Burns in November 2021. Russia launched its war against Ukraine three months later in February 2022. 

Tuesday's talks came as truce negotiations between the US and Iran have stalled. Moscow had previously offered to act as a broker between the two parties over the conflict.

entries.title: Gamescom 2026 highlights gaming industry's strength, AI challenges
entries.summary: Gamescom 2026 opens in Cologne as the global gaming industry continues to grow. But rising hardware costs, AI concerns and slowing user growth all pose challenges.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

Gamescom 2026 opens in Cologne as the global gaming industry continues to grow. But rising hardware costs, AI concerns and slowing user growth all pose challenges.

Earlier this month, gaming giant Electronic Arts was sold to an investment consortium including Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, for $55 billion (€47 billion).

The deal stood out in a few ways. It is believed to be one of the largest leveraged buyouts in history, meaning a significant chunk of the $55 billion was borrowed money that the company itself will have to pay back.

It was also the second-biggest deal in gaming history, after Microsoft's purchase of Activision Blizzard, the company behind the "Call of Duty" franchise, for $69 billion in 2023.

The Electronic Arts sale additionally shone a light on the growing economic significance of the gaming industry and the increasing interest from major global investors such as Saudi Arabia, seeking to benefit from the sector's cultural and financial clout.

Gamescom — a massive global gathering

That cultural and financial clout will be on full display over the next few days in the German city of Cologne, where Gamescom, the world's largest gaming event and trade fair, takes place.

The event attracts thousands of exhibitors and games developers, close to half a million visitors and many more millions of fans connecting online from around the world.

It's the place where companies build hype for their upcoming releases, with massive rooms packed with screens, consoles and a range of gaming experiences.

"Gamescom is a very useful barometer for the health and mindset of the industry," Piers Harding-Rolls, a games industry analyst with Ampere, told DW.

That health looks fairly robust at present.

The global games market is currently valued at $213.9 billion, up 6.1% year on year, according to Newzoo, a gaming industry market analysis company. Manu Rosier, the company's director of market intelligence, says that growth is broad across the sector's three main platforms: mobile, console and PC.

It now comfortably rivals the movie and music businesses both in terms of finances and, some would argue, cultural significance and reach.

"If you add the music subscription and transactional markets together with the cinema box office, spending on games is over three times bigger," said Harding-Rolls.

Joost van Dreunen, an assistant professor at NYU Stern School of Business and the author of "One Up: Creativity, Competition, and the Global Business of Video Games," says gaming's communal aspects have powered its growth.

"The cultural relevance of interactive entertainment has substantially expanded in the past few years, as millions of players around the world have found a common interest in playing together online," he told DW. "That's something few other forms of entertainment have accomplished."

AI creates new challenges for gaming

Yet the sector faces significant challenges. Like most industries, it is grappling with artificial intelligence (AI) and an onslaught of AI-generated material.

"AI is flooding the existing digital markets with content that is generally disregarded by players," said van Dreunen. "It nevertheless makes it more difficult for audiences to find relevant content in an expanding sea of slop."

There is already clear evidence of resistance from gamers toward AI. A recent survey by Quantic Foundry, a gaming analytics company, found that 85% of respondents had a less than neutral position on generative AI.

Another challenge AI is bringing to the gaming industry is cost related. The development of AI infrastructure and data centers has led to a surge in demand for chips and memory, which has driven prices up. Nvidia recently warned some of its largest customers that semiconductor prices would increase by as much as 15%.

That has driven up component costs for the gaming sector. "It shows on every platform. PC builds and upgrades, console prices climbing mid-cycle rather than falling as they did in past generations, and rising smartphone prices," said Rosier.

He thinks the increased costs could delay the introduction of the next generation of games console in the next few years, while Piers Harding-Rolls thinks it is adding pressure to a sector grappling with other financial concerns.

"Increasing costs for games hardware components pushing up prices, hyper-competition across all areas of the market meaning a glut of content, and challenges in discovery (of new users) and user acquisition," he said.

Joost van Dreunen also cautions that the sector is now more dominated by the biggest players than in previous years, with major releases this year such as the latest "Grand Theft Auto" and Marvel's "Wolverine" helping boost overall revenues.

"Demand is more top-heavy than in the boom years, which makes it really strong at the top and precarious in the middle," he said.

Another challenge is keeping gamers gaming and adding new ones. Manu Rosier says there are now 3.7 billion gamers around the world, more than 40% of the global population and more than 60% of all those who use the internet. However, there are signs that new user growth is slowing, he says.

Gaming enters a new phase of growth

Yet as the industry gathers in Cologne, there is an unmistakable optimism about its prospects. Beyond the gloom around AI, there is the belief that technology could also significantly reduce costs.

"AI is being used across games companies to replace repetitive tasks that are better done by agents including preproduction work and coding. This saves time and hopefully delivers efficiency, with the aim of cutting cost," said Harding-Rolls.

As for its ability to improve gameplay, many gamers remain doubtful. That's in part because the definition of a "gamer" has shifted, which has helped the industry itself evolve.

"A generation ago, games were predominantly single-player focused and narrative-driven. Today, games are more social and less focused on story," said van Dreunen.

Yet that in turn brings its own challenge, with developers competing for the attention of billions of gamers around the world in a more crowded market.

"The market is continually evolving and reinventing itself," added Harding-Rolls. "Companies are continually challenged to innovate and bring new experiences to consumers."

Edited by: Tim Rooks

entries.title: India: Assam tea industry faces climate-driven labor crisis
entries.summary: Plantations in Assam produce more than half of India's tea. But rising heat is hurting yields, workers are increasingly leaving for more stable work, and producers are feeling the squeeze of stagnant tea prices.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

Plantations in Assam produce more than half of India's tea. But rising heat is hurting yields, workers are increasingly leaving for more stable work, and producers are feeling the squeeze of stagnant tea prices.

The problems facing upper Assam's tea gardens are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore for workers like Bidesh Kamar and Sumitra Tanti.

Recent floods disrupted work for weeks in the northeast Indian state, adding even more uncertainty to their already precarious livelihood. More than 50 tea gardens were damaged following a devastating storm that swept across parts of Assam.

"Life has become unpredictable," Tanti told DW.

"The weather can disrupt work, while wages remain low and work is not as dependable as it once was," she added.

Kamar said the economics of tea have changed.

"Tea is not as profitable as it once was, and there is less certainty about the work," Kamar told DW.

After 15 years working tea plantations, Kamar is now considering whether it is time to "move on to greener pastures."

Assam's dwindling tea workforce

Their experience points to a growing problem for Assam's tea industry. With the business becoming less profitable and working conditions more uncertain, the industry is struggling to retain the experienced workforce which forms the backbone of the state's tea production.

Assam produces about 52% of India's tea and supports around 700,000 plantation workers and 140,000 small tea growers.

For generations, it's tea plantations have depended on a vast workforce picking leaves by hand.

But that model is now under pressure as the climate gets hotter, tea becomes less profitable and locals increasingly look elsewhere for work.

Oversupply has pushed prices down, while higher wages, fertilizer and fuel costs are squeezing producers.

Sanjiv Gogoi, who owns the 400-acre (162-hectares) Sanjiv Tea estate, said tea producers are grappling with a whole range of problems.

"Productivity has fallen, and the labor supply is not always reliable. More workers are leaving the plantations because the work no longer pays enough," Gogoi told DW.

The pressure is even greater on small growers, who produce nearly half of Assam's tea, he said.

"They have little bargaining power and often have to sell their freshly picked leaves to factories at low prices."

A changing landscape for tea

At the same time, erratic rainfall, rising temperatures and new pests are reducing yields and making traditional tea-growing areas increasingly vulnerable.

In Assam's major tea-growing districts, temperatures now regularly reach 36°C to 40°C (+100° F), putting both tea plants and workers under severe heat stress.

Research shows that every 1°C rise in temperature can reduce tea yields by about 87 kilos per hectare in India.

For tea workers, who spend hours outdoors picking leaves, extreme heat adds another physical strain to already demanding work, with dehydration, exhaustion and fainting reported during the hottest hours.

Tea deflation drives workers away

According to statistics from India's North Eastern Tea Association (NETA), tea prices have barely kept pace with the rising cost of producing the crop. More over, labor costs now account for roughly 60% of all production costs, leaving plantations squeezed between rising wages and weak prices.

This has created a labor crisis. Plantation workers earn around 250 to 280 Indian Rupees (€2.30–€2.60 or $2.63-$2.94) a day, while unions are demanding 350 to 500 to reflect the rising cost of living.

"The most fundamental concern is the widening gap between the cost of producing tea and the price we realize from the market," Bidyananda Barkakoty, tea farmer adviser at NETA and former vice-chairman of the Tea Board of India told DW.

He warned the departure of experienced workers was affecting both productivity and quality. Good tea depends on careful plucking of the right leaves, something that becomes harder when experienced workers are in short supply.

Meanwhile, absenteeism in some tea growing districts has reportedly reached more than 50%, as workers choose construction, urban jobs or government employment schemes that offer better and faster returns.

New machines 'a necessity' for Assam's tea industry

Harkirat Singh Sidhu, a veteran tea planter with more than 55 years of experience across plantations in nine countries, says Assam's industry must adapt.

"We need to make the changes and not be pushed into making changes," Sidhu told DW.

He predicted that labor issues will only grow worse, "making mechanization a necessity rather than an option."

Sidhu advocates for regenerative farming to build resilient soil, combined with upgraded drainage networks, shade canopy management, and reduced reliance on chemical pesticides.

"Everything around us has changed, and so we need to seriously think out the changes we need to work out," he added.

As experienced workers leave the tea industry, estates increasingly rely on temporary or mechanical harvesting, which can reduce quality and prices further.

The result is a difficult downward spiral. Falling productivity reduces revenues, leaving estates with less money to invest in replanting, irrigation and measures to cope with the changing climate.

That, in turn, makes the industry even less attractive to workers.

"The younger generation will stay only when they see a future in the tea gardens, not merely a job," said Barkakoty.

That means better incomes and living conditions for workers, but also offering them skilled jobs through mechanization and technology.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Deadly flash flood wipes away villages in Nepal, Tibet
entries.summary: Hundreds of people were reported missing, including 291 international tourists. Rescue helicopters have been unable to land in affected areas due to high floodwaters.
entries.content:
Nepal

Deadly flash flood wipes away villages in Nepal, Tibet

August 26, 2026

Hundreds of people were reported missing, including 291 international tourists. Rescue helicopters have been unable to land in affected areas due to high floodwaters.

Several people were confirmed dead and hundreds more are missing after a flash flood swept through remote valleys in Nepal and Tibet on Wedensday.

The floodwaters washed away villages, damaged bridges and destroyed electrical infrastructure on both sides of the Nepal-China border.

"There is devastation everywhere we look," ‌Tula ​Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa district, told Reuters.

"The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing."

At 8 people were killed in Nepal while Chinese authorities also reported that a mudslide caused "major casualties" on the other side of the border in Tibet.

Hundreds of people missing

Nepal's Tourism Board said 384 travelers were reported missing.

Among those missing travelers were including 291 foreign nationals, inculding 105 Indians.

A Nepali police spokesperson told Germany's DPA news agency that dozens of personnel were also missing.

"So far, we only have confirmation of 26 police personnel who remain missing in the flood," they said.

"We also have missing information of government revenue officials, hydropower workers among others. But we are still collecting the data."

What caused the flash floods?

Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said an earthquake triggered an avalanche in the Himalayas that then triggered flash floods in the valleys below.

Chinese state news agency Xinhua said a mudslide on the Nepali side of the mountains spread to Gyirong County in Tibet.

Major rescue operations underway

Nepal dispatched more than a dozen rescue helicopters to the mountainous Rasuwa region, but floodwaters were too high for the helicopters to land.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the military and police were assisting with rescues.

"Instructions have been given ... to move ​the people living in the lower areas ⁠to safer places," he said. "People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert."

Chinese President Xi Jinping also ordered an "all out" rescue effort.

He said "the most urgent task is doing everything possible to search for and rescue the missing people... quickly treat injured people and minimize casualties to the greatest extent possible," according to Chinese state media.

A second flood may be imminent, according to Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.

"With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur," he told the AFP news agency.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Germany: Carnivalgoers rescued after being trapped on ride
entries.summary: Passengers became stranded high up in the air after a swing carousel malfunctioned in Hamburg.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Carnivalgoers rescued after being trapped on ride

August 26, 2026

Passengers became stranded high up in the air after a swing carousel malfunctioned in Hamburg.

Nearly two dozen carnivalgoers were rescued after a 90 minute ordeal in central Hamburg late on Tuesday, having been stuck 25 meters (82 feet) in the air on a swing carousel ride.

The Hamburger Dom carnival is held in the St.Pauli area of the city three times a year, and is one of Germany's longest-running and most well-visited fun fairs, attracting some 10 million guests annually.

On Tuesday evening, 23 passengers become stuck partly up the 70-meter (230-foot) ride when it malfunctioned and stopped moving.

Firefighters arrived at the scene, erecting ladders to bring down each guest individually.

Authorities said that no one needed medical attention, but that the ride would remain closed through Sunday when the carnival concludes.

entries.title: Germany news: Sugar tax plan leaves sour taste
entries.summary: Germany's plans for a sugar tax are facing growing opposition amid claims that it's more about raising revenue than health. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Sugar tax plan leaves sour taste

Published August 26, 2026last updated August 26, 2026

Germany's plans for a sugar tax are facing growing opposition amid claims that it's more about raising revenue than health. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Germany's proposed sugar tax is facing opposition from both inside and outside the ruling coalition
  • Environmentalist Greens question the purpose of the levy and conservative politicians warn it could add to everyday costs
  • Meanwhile, German Cabinet members, including Chancellor Friedrich Merz, are meeting for a second day at Neuhardenberg Castle in Brandenburg
  • Germany's exporters are feeling more confident about future sales abroad

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, August 26, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Dobrindt warns of rising hybrid threats to Germany

Dobrindt warns of rising hybrid threats to Germany

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has warned that hybrid attacks on Germany are likely to intensify. He said new security laws should be adopted before the end of the year.

Dobrindt said the threat from sabotage, espionage and covert operations by foreign powers had been discussed at the government's cabinet retreat in Neuhardenberg.

"We want to swiftly implement the security laws that we consider necessary this year," he said.

Dobrindt said some of the measures had been politically disputed for decades, but argued that agreement within the coalition showed the government was capable of acting in response to new security threats.

The plans include strengthening Germany's intelligence services, which Dobrindt has said should be transformed into more operationally capable secret services.

His comments come after the discovery of a drone and explosives at Leipzig Airport near Ukrainian cargo aircraft.

According to information from security sources cited in the report, parts of another drone and further explosives have since been found.

Dobrindt said such incidents were part of a broader hybrid threat involving sabotage, espionage and covert action by foreign powers.

"They occupy me almost every day, or every day, and certainly our coalition every week," he said.

Skip next section Carnival ride leaves visitors stranded

Carnival ride leaves visitors stranded

Nearly two dozen people were rescued after spending 90 minutes stuck in the air on a swing carousel at Hamburg's famous Dom carnival.

Read more here about what happened.

Skip next section Klingbeil: 'Tech bros' should not decide AI's future

Klingbeil: 'Tech bros' should not decide AI's future

Germany's Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has warned against allowing Silicon Valley tech leaders to determine the future of artificial intelligence, as Germany seeks to strengthen its technological independence.

"It should not be the tech bros in Silicon Valley, with their dangerous ideology, who decide the future of artificial intelligence," Klingbeil said following a cabinet retreat.

"We can act as Europeans and as Germany. We have every opportunity and every chance to put the best solutions in place."

Klingbeil said the government's economic push would focus on "new economic growth and good, secure jobs."

"If we want to create prosperity for the future in Germany, these are the two cornerstones," he said.

Klingbeil said it was crucial that Germany and Europe become more technologically independent and that the jobs created by emerging industries remain in the country.

"It is crucial that the jobs of the future are created in Germany," he said.

"It is also crucial that we become more independent and sovereign, so that decisions about our future are not made only in Washington or Beijing."

Skip next section Merz puts AI at center of Germany's economic push

Merz puts AI at center of Germany's economic push

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said artificial intelligence will play a central role in the government's efforts to modernize the German economy.

"Whether in industry, skilled trades, small and medium-sized businesses, defense, medicine, pharmaceuticals or medical technology, Germany has enormous, previously unimagined opportunities here," Merz said following a cabinet retreat.

"AI — artificial intelligence — is a catalyst for a new beginning, for a modern Germany."

Merz said AI was about more than productivity and jobs.

"This is not only about work, value creation and the future. It is also about sovereignty for our society, for our way of life and, not least, for our security."

The chancellor also pledged that the coalition would press ahead with reforms agreed before the summer break, including changes to pensions, taxation, healthcare and bureaucracy.

"Our message is: we have embarked on major reforms. We will implement them, and we will lead our country into a good future," Merz said.

Skip next section Merz says Germany is returning to growth after years of stagnation

Merz says Germany is returning to growth after years of stagnation

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said Germany is emerging from three years of economic stagnation and recession, as his government pledged to focus on growth, jobs and innovation.

Speaking after a cabinet retreat, Merz pointed to a surprisingly strong rise in the Ifo business climate index in August, improving growth figures and a high number of new business start-ups as evidence that confidence was returning.

"The business climate index rose surprisingly strongly in August, and that was the fourth increase in a row," Merz said.

"The economy is already growing in the third quarter, with good figures. Forecasts for 2027 are being revised upward."

"We have three years of recession behind us, and now we are growing again," he added.

Merz said the improvement was taking place despite the wars in Ukraine and Iran along with continuing international trade tensions.

"We are seeing impressive numbers of new business start-ups," he said.

"Young people, young women and young men, are founding companies in Germany in numbers we have never seen before, and traditional companies are once again daring to invest and try something new."

Skip next section German exporters most optimistic since 2022

German exporters most optimistic since 2022

German exporters have become more optimistic about their prospects than at any point in more than four years, according to a survey by the Ifo economic institute.

Ifo's export expectations index jumped to 9.6 points in August, up from -2.8 in July. The institute said it was the highest reading since February 2022 and the sharpest monthly increase since June 2020.

"The export economy is gaining momentum," Ifo survey chief Klaus Wohlrabe said.

He said exports to the European Union were particularly strong, while business with China remained weak.

Companies producing electrical equipment, computers, electronics and optical products were among the most optimistic.

Ifo linked the improvement partly to increasing digitalization and heavy investment in artificial intelligence.

Even Germany's struggling automotive sector reported much stronger confidence about future exports.

The brighter export outlook follows stronger-than-expected economic data.

Germany's gross domestic product grew by 0.3% in the second quarter compared with the previous three months, the Federal Statistical Office said Tuesday, slightly above its initial estimate.

Skip next section German ministers start Cabinet retreat day with cycling and jogging

German ministers start Cabinet retreat day with cycling and jogging

Several German ministers have started the second day of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Cabinet retreat in Brandenburg with an early-morning workout.

Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil and Environment Minister Carsten Schneider, both from the center-left Social Democratic Party, set off on racing bikes from Neuhardenberg Palace shortly after sunrise.

The pair covered 26 kilometers (16 miles) in one hour and 45 minutes through the surrounding countryside.

"An age-appropriate pace for the terrain," joked Schneider, who is 50. Klingbeil is two years younger.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Health Minister Carsten Linnemann, both from the center-right Christian Democratic Union, opted for a run around the palace grounds instead.

The two-day retreat, which began Tuesday, is focusing on the effects of the summer heatwave and Germany's economic competitiveness.

Startup founders and Jörg Dittrich, president of Germany's skilled crafts association, are also taking part in discussions.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Klingbeil and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt are due to present the retreat's conclusions at 12:30 p.m.

Skip next section Which products could be subject to the sugar tax?

Which products could be subject to the sugar tax?

Despite being widely described as a "sugar tax," the proposal is aimed at drinks containing sugar or sweeteners, rather than sweets or other sugary foods.

A Finance Ministry paper suggests the levy could apply not only to soft drinks but also to:

  • Juices
  • Milk-based drinks
  • Iced tea
  • Beer-based mixed drinks
  • Oat and soya drinks
  • Ready-made coffee drinks
  • Alcohol-free beer and wine

The paper also floated taxing zero- and light drinks containing artificial sweeteners. But Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has now ruled that out.

"I won't do that. It won't happen," Klingbeil said on Instagram, adding that a "sugar tax on sugar-free drinks" made no sense.

He stressed that the leaked paper was only an internal working document and had neither been politically agreed nor approved by the coalition.

Pure milk and 100% fruit juice were listed as exempt in the draft. The final scope of any tax therefore remains unsettled.

Skip next section Opposition grows to Germany's planned sugar tax

Opposition grows to Germany's planned sugar tax

Political opposition to Germany's planned sugar tax has widened, with criticism now coming from both the Greens and the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Green Party co-leader Felix Banaszak said he supported a sugar tax in principle but feared the proposal was being used primarily to plug holes in the federal budget.

Banaszak said the original purpose of such a tax should be to reduce health risks linked to high sugar consumption and the resulting costs for the health system.

"My impression is that an instrument we fundamentally support is now simply being used to plug budget holes," he told Welt TV, adding that using the tax mainly as a revenue-raising measure could undermine public support for it.

Hesse's State Premier Boris Rhein of the CDU has called for the plan to be dropped altogether.

"At a time when many people are struggling with high prices, the state must not make food and drinks even more expensive," Rhein said.

He argued that the government should instead focus on lower energy prices, reduced social security contributions and easing everyday living costs.

The Agriculture Ministry has also expressed reservations about the current proposal, while other CDU lawmakers have criticized its scope.

Consumer groups and Foodwatch support the idea, while food and beverage industry associations remain strongly opposed.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom in Bonn.

You join us as Germany’s planned sugar tax is proving politically unpalatable, with criticism now coming from both the Greens and the conservative Christian Democrats.

Meanwhile, German Cabinet members, including Chancellor Friedrich Merz, are meeting for a second day at Neuhardenberg Castle in Brandenburg. German ministers are expected to brief reporters on the outcome of the meetings.

Also, German exporters are sounding more upbeat than they have in years.

The Ifo economic institute says the export economy is “gaining momentum,” with demand from the European Union looking especially strong.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of what Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: NYC: Mamdani opposes rally with Hindu nationalist leader
entries.summary: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced opposition to an upcoming event featuring RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat, calling the Hindu nationalist group's ideology "exclusionary" while acknowledging the city can't block a private event.
entries.content:
India

NYC: Mamdani opposes rally with Hindu nationalist leader

August 26, 2026

NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced opposition to an upcoming event featuring RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat, calling the Hindu nationalist group's ideology "exclusionary" while acknowledging the city can't block a private event.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday he does not support an upcoming event featuring Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Hindu nationalist group Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), though he acknowledged the city likely has no power to stop it.

Bhagwat is scheduled to speak Saturday at Madison Square Garden as part of what organizers are calling the "Universal Oneness Celebration," an event expected to draw around 5,000 attendees, local media reported. It is part of a broader global outreach tour tied to the RSS's centenary year, wherein Bhagwat is visiting the United States, Canada and the UK. 

What did Mamdani say?

When asked whether the event should be canceled at a press conference, Mamdani said: "I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on canceling a private event."

Mamdani is the first Muslim and Indian American mayor in New York City's history. He added that his opposition to the visit reflected his role leading a city that believes in "the belonging of each and every person, no matter their color, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from." 

His mother is acclaimed Indian filmmaker Mira Nair. He added that he grew up with an understanding of India as "a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India."

"It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision."

Who is organizing the event?

The event is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, which says it has backing from over 135 Hindu American organizations and is meant to promote shared heritage and interfaith unity.

However, several interfaith and civil rights groups – including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York – have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history. They held a news conference outside New York City Hall calling for the event to be canceled.

"Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Hindus. He leads an extremist Hindu nationalist movement that has fueled violence, exclusion and fear for minority communities," said Sravya Tadepalli, Deputy Executive Director of Hindus for Human Rights, in a statement. "New York should not provide the RSS with a stage on which religious nationalism can be repackaged as unity."

What is the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh and how is it related to PM Modi?

The RSS is a right-wing Hindu organization founded by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar in 1925. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for National Volunteer Organization. The group describes itself as a "Hindu centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus and disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance.

The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization. 

In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities.

Rights organizations decry rise in abuses against religious minorities

However, days earlier, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom urged sanctions against the RSS and asked the American government not to extend diplomatic courtesies to RSS members. The US government advisory body called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims."

United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more.

India's BJP-led government denies any discriminatory intent, pointing to programs such as food subsidies and electrification initiatives, which it says benefit all communities.

The organization has been banned in India on multiple occasions, including in 1948 after a Hindu nationalist who had ties with the RSS assassinated independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.

entries.title: Pakistan: Islamabad hospital fire kills at least 14 infants
entries.summary: A fire broke out in the third floor of a maternity ward in Islamabad. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has called for an immediate investigation into the tragedy.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan: Islamabad hospital fire kills at least 14 infants

August 26, 2026

A fire broke out in the third floor of a maternity ward in Islamabad. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has called for an immediate investigation into the tragedy.

A least 14 infants were killed after a fire broke out at the maternity ward of a hospital in Islamabad, Pakistan, on Wednesday.

"A fire broke out on the third floor of the MCH Ward at PIMS Hospital," the district office of Islamabad said, referring to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences.

The blaze broke out at around 6:45 a.m. (0145 UTC) when an air conditioning unit exploded inside the nursery, rescuers said.

Officials said 16 newborns were in the ward at the time, adding that one was rescued.

Outside the hospital, a nurse read out the names of babies who had perished as their families gathered around.

"I lost my daughter. She was only three days old," one father told the AFP news agency.

"My wife was in the ward. They took everyone out. We were sitting on the road waiting for help."

Investigation underway

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an immediate investigation into the incident.

"A tragedy involving children is an irreparable loss," he said in a statement.

"Those ​responsible should be identified, and ​the strictest action should be taken."

The incident is one of the deadliest hospital fires in recent memory in Pakistan, where healthcare is subsidized but public hospitals are often are under-resourced and overburdened.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Why landmines are back in force despite international bans
entries.summary: Russia's war on Ukraine has prompted several European countries to abandon a landmark 1990s landmine treaty. DW examines what is at stake.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

Russia's war on Ukraine has prompted several European countries to abandon a landmark 1990s landmine treaty. DW examines what is at stake.

Raheela Bibi was outside playing with her siblings when a landmine exploded. It was August 2020 and she was 12, living in Pakistan. Both her hands were amputated after the incident. Her sister suffered a serious leg injury, while her brother's eye was hurt. Bibi told DW in 2023 that though it was extremely difficult for her to do her homework, she was determined to continue with her education.

In 2025, more than 5,000 people, mainly civilians, were killed or injured by landmines or unexploded ordnance according to a preliminary analysis by the NGO Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor. In South Sudan, 90% of the victims last year were children.

Landmines are actually designed to injure adults not kill them. This is because an injured soldier is more of a strain on an enemy country's resources than a dead soldier. But in peacetime, landmines continue to pose a deadly threat not only to soldiers but to civilians and particularly children, who often die.

Decades after the brutal conflicts from 1991 to 2001 that were Yugoslav wars, people continue to be killed and injured by landmines in former Yugoslavia, particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina.

What is the Ottawa Treaty?

In 1999, there were approximately 25,000 landmine casualties per year. This prompted pressure to ban the use of anti-personnel landmines. In 1997, representatives from more than 120 countries signed the Ottawa Treaty, which became legally binding in 1999. In total, 166 countries ratified the treaty, but not China, India, Russia or the US.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, five European NATO countries, which share a border with Russia, have withdrawn from the treaty. Ukraine has also withdrawn though this will not take legal effect until the war ends.

"This is a dangerous precedent that European states, of all countries, have set," Simone Wisotzki from the Frankfurt-based Leibniz Peace Research Institute (PRIF) told DW. "Other parties to the Ottawa Treaty, which could also face equally extreme situations in times of conflict, could take the same step. We would then have to deal with more withdrawals, which would, of course, undermine the legitimacy of the entire treaty."

Last year, Ukraine withdrew from the treaty and justified the move citing the actions of Russia, which has never ratified the treaty and has been using mines in Ukrainian territory. "We cannot remain bound under conditions when the enemy has no restrictions," said Roman Kostenko, the secretary of the Ukrainian parliament's committee on national security, defense and intelligence.

If a country isn't at war, its withdrawal from the Ottawa Treaty is supposed to take effect six months after its announcement. If it is at war, however, withdrawal should take effect only after a peace treaty has been signed. Despite the legal uncertainty, Ukraine is reportedly already using mines, albeit on a much smaller scale than Russia.

A quarter of Ukraine affected by landmines

According the United Nations Mine Action Service (UNMAS), as of mid-2025 approximately 25% of Ukraine was affected by landmines and explosive ordnance. This applied not only to Ukrainian-controlled territories but also to Russian-occupied areas in the east and southeast of the country.

"Since February 2022, over 1,150 civilians have been killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW)," UNMAS writes on its website, pointing out that the cost of full demining is estimated at just under $35 billion (approx. €30 billion) over 10 years.

Poland, Finland (which joined NATO after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine), Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, which have all suffered from Russian aggression and occupation in the past, also decided to withdraw from the Ottawa Treaty last year.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has stated on several occasions that his country wants to be able to mine its eastern borders with Russia very quickly if need be. The state-owned Polish defense company Belma has been contracted to produce anti-personnel mines in large quantities. Lithuania has also announced that it will resume the manufacture and purchase of landmines.

The Finnish military has said that if mines are necessary, they should be laid responsibly, accurate maps of their position must be created and there should be precise plans for demining.

Wisotzki from PRIF said that this is progress compared to the past but that modern anti-personnel mines often have integrated sensors and smart technologies that make it difficult to remove and destroy the mines.

"That's why I'm very critical of this and say that even new technologies present problems that, in turn, make mine clearance more difficult. In practice, mines are always laid in areas that are also used by civilians. They then remain in those territories and then injure civilians disproportionately."

In its reports, the Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor has pointed out that while mines that were laid during past conflicts continued to be cleared, mines continue to be laid in Ukraine or in other countries such as Myanmar.

Where does global arms control stand?

This comes at a time when there is increasingly less arms control. In the past few years, three major agreements between the United States and Russia have expired or been terminated: the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty that banned all nuclear and conventional ground-launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and missile launchers with intermediate range; the New Start Treaty which is a nuclear arms reduction treaty; and the Treaty on Open Skies, which set out the framework for a regime of observation flights over the territory of participating states.

In 2023, Russia's withdrawal also effectively put an end to the CFE treaty that aimed to create a secure and stable balance of conventional armed forces in Europe and to remove the capability to launch surprise attacks or large-scale offensives

"Humanitarian arms control — which includes the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention — was in effect the only area that could still be said to be working," Wisotzki said. "And that is no longer the case."

This article was originally published in German.
